characterization_methods.purpose: reveal grain boundaries and precipitates for metallographic inspection
characterization_methods.technique: optical microscopy after etching in alcoholic 10% nitric acid solution

characterization_methods.key_findings: Polycrystalline Fe-12%Al: real Al content 12.0 at.% (6.2 wt.-%); impurities C 50–60 wt.ppm, Si 60–90 wt.ppm, Cu <40 wt.ppm (Table 1, polycrystal 12).

defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: Deformation of the furnace-cooled Fe-12%Al initiated cell formation: thick dark cell walls of high dislocation density enclosing lighter, nearly dislocation-free cell interiors (Fig. 6(b)), indicating sufficient dislocation mobility in the furnace-cooled state.

interfaces.interface_notes: The thin carbides were observed only on grain boundaries in the polycrystals, appearing after slow furnace cooling from 1100 °C (or prolonged 14-day anneals at 320 °C) and believed to form from the up-to-80-ppm carbon content.

comparative_performance.comparison_metric: The Fe-12%Al alloy (60 ppm C) showed only a weak effect of quenching on its deformation behaviour, whereas the Fe-16%Al alloy (<20 ppm C) showed a strong effect of quenching.

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Binary Fe-12%Al prepared by vacuum induction melting in Al2O3 crucibles using Fe with 99.99% purity (zone-melting purified) and Al with 99.999% purity; solidified in Cu moulds to rods usually with 18 mm diameter.

Specimens were heat-treated at 1100 °C usually only 15 min; for heat treatments other than those up to 300 °C the specimens were enclosed in evacuated (10^-6 bar) SiO2 capsules. This is the solution/annealing step preceding the furnace cooling of the Fe-12%Al (Fig. 6: quench/furnace cool from 1100 °C).

Furnace cooling from 1100 °C to room temperature (the defining process of this sample, proc_fc-1100-rt). Slow furnace cooling produced fine thin platelike or rod-like precipitates (carbides) on grain boundaries of the polycrystals.
5.5% compressive straining at 10^-4 s^-1 rate at room temperature, applied to the furnace-cooled Fe-12%Al to produce the deformation substructure studied by TEM.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: compression test; 5.5% compressive straining; specimen surfaces cleansed by grinding

precipitates.distribution: on grain boundaries (after slow furnace cooling from 1100 °C)

structures.overall_structure: Polycrystalline Fe-12%Al (real 12.0 at.%, 6.2 wt.-%, 60 ppm C) with a coarse grain structure (grain size of the order of 1 mm). Slow furnace cooling from 1100 °C produced fine thin platelike or rod-like precipitates (believed to be carbides) on the grain boundaries. Before deformation nearly no dislocations were present; after 5.5% compressive straining at 10^-4 s^-1 at room temperature the furnace-cooled alloy developed a dislocation cell structure.

unmapped_findings: Polycrystalline Fe-12%Al has a real composition of 12.0 at.% (6.2 wt.-%) Al with impurity contents C 50–60 wt.ppm, Si 60–90 wt.ppm and Cu <40 wt.ppm (Table 1, polycrystal 12; nominal 12).
The Fe-12%Al alloy (60 ppm C) showed only a weak effect of quenching, in contrast to the Fe-16%Al alloy (<20 ppm C) which showed a strong effect of quenching.
Before deformation only few straight dislocations were observed in the quenched Fe-12%Al, whereas nearly no dislocations were observed in the furnace-cooled alloy.

The carbides are believed to form from the presence of up to 80 ppm carbon; their amount was smaller for lower C contents, and only rare tiny precipitate particles were detected on grain boundaries of an alloy with only 20 ppm C after furnace cooling.
The compressed Fe-12%Al specimens were deformed by 5.5% compressive straining at 10^-4 s^-1 rate at room temperature for the TEM study (Fig. 6).
